Was it that this old carpenter had been a lifelong wanderer, whose much rolling to and fro had not only gathered no moss but, what is more, had rubbed off whatever small outward attachments might originally have belonged to him? You might almost say that this strange uncompromisedness in him involved a sort of unintelligence; for in his numerous trades he did not seem to work so much by reason or by instinct, or simply because he had been taught to, or by any mixture of all these, even or uneven, but merely by a kind of deaf-and-dumb, spontaneous, literal process. He was a pure manipulator, a worker with the hands; his brain, if he had ever had one, must have oozed early on into the muscles of his fingers. He was like one of those unreasoning but still highly useful Sheffield contrivances, multum in parvo (much in little), which have the outside — though a little swollen — of a common pocketknife, but contain not only blades of various sizes but also screwdrivers, corkscrews, tweezers, awls, pens, rulers, nail-files, and countersinks. So if his superiors wanted to use the carpenter as a screwdriver, all they had to do was open that part of him, and the screw was fast; or if as tweezers, pick him up by the legs, and there they were.

items.reason: Nickname changed: 'you old Smut' (the sooty blacksmith) became 'you old Blacksmith'; 'his old Mogulship' became 'his old lordship', losing the Mogul joke; 'calves of legs' garbled to 'calf-legs'.
items.new: Drat the file, and drat the bone! What should be soft is hard, and what should be hard is soft. That's how it goes for us who file old jaws and shinbones. Let's try another. Aye, now, this works better (sneezes). Hello, this bone dust is (sneezes) — why it's (sneezes) — yes it's (sneezes) — bless my soul, it won't let me speak! This is what an old fellow gets now for working in dead lumber. Saw a live tree and you don't get this dust; amputate a live bone and you don't get it (sneezes). Come, come, you old Smut, there, lend a hand, and let's have that ferrule and buckle-screw; I'll be ready for them in a minute. Lucky now (sneezes) there's no knee-joint to make; that might puzzle me a little; but a mere shinbone — why, it's as easy as making hop-poles; only I'd like to put a good finish on it. Time, time; if I only had the time, I could turn him out as neat a leg now as ever (sneezes) scraped to a lady in a parlor. Those buckskin legs and calves I've seen in shop windows wouldn't compare at all. They soak up water, they do; and of course they get rheumatic and have to be doctored (sneezes) with washes and lotions, just like live legs. There; before I saw it off, now, I must call his old Mogulship and see whether the length will be all right; too short, if anything, I guess. Ha! That's the heel; we're in luck; here he comes, or it's somebody else, that's certain.

items.reason: The carpenter's sea-metaphor 'a dismasted man never entirely loses the feeling of his old spar' was literalized to 'dismembered man ... old limb'; 'if it be really so' left archaic.
items.new: Truly, sir, I begin to understand somewhat now. Yes, I have heard something curious on that score, sir; how a dismasted man never entirely loses the feeling of his old spar, but it will still be pricking him at times. May I humbly ask if that is really so, sir?

items.reason: 'standing there in thy spite' (in spite of you) mistranslated as 'in your very space'; 'uninterpenetratingly' (without mingling with you) dropped; 'why may not you' left archaic.
items.new: Hush, then. How do you know that some entire, living, thinking thing may not be standing invisibly, and without mingling with you, exactly where you are standing now; aye, and standing there in spite of you? In your most solitary hours, then, don't you fear eavesdroppers? Hold on, don't speak! And if I still feel the sting of my crushed leg, though it has now been dissolved so long, then why might not you, carpenter, feel the fiery pains of hell forever, and without a body? Hah!

items.reason: 'the wealthiest Prætorians at the auction of the Roman empire' lost 'Praetorians' (the guard who auctioned the empire); '(which was the world's)' changed to 'which was the world'.
items.new: Bungle away at it then, and bring it to me (turns to go). Oh, Life! Here I am, proud as a Greek god, and yet standing in debt to this blockhead for a bone to stand on! Cursed be that mortal indebtedness of each to all, which will not do away with ledgers. I would be as free as air; and I'm down in the whole world's books. I am so rich I could have matched bid for bid with the wealthiest Praetorians at the auction of the Roman empire (which was the world's); and yet I owe for the flesh in the tongue I brag with. By heavens! I'll get a crucible, and get into it, and dissolve myself down to one small, compendious vertebra. So.

items.reason: 'the water chucks you under the chin' became 'chokes you under the chin'; 'roly-poly old coach-horses' lost 'roly-poly'; 'spavined the other for life' (lamed, as a horse) flattened to 'broken'; 'you Smut' renamed 'you Blacksmith'.
items.new: Well, well, well! Stubb knows him best of all, and Stubb always says he's queer; says nothing but that one sufficient little word queer; he's queer, says Stubb; he's queer — queer, queer; and keeps dinning it into Mr. Starbuck all the time — queer, sir, queer, queer, very queer. And here's his leg! Yes, now that I think of it, here's his bedfellow! Has a stick of whale's jawbone for a wife! And this is his leg; he'll stand on this. What was that now about one leg standing in three places, and all three places standing in one hell — how was that? Oh! I don't wonder he looked so scornful at me! I'm sort of strange-thoughted sometimes, they say; but that's only haphazard-like. Then, a short little old body like me should never try to wade out into deep waters with tall, heron-built captains; the water chucks you under the chin pretty quick, and there's a great cry for lifeboats. And here's the heron's leg! Long and slim, sure enough! Now, for most folks one pair of legs lasts a lifetime, and that must be because they use them mercifully, the way a tender-hearted old lady uses her roly-poly old coach-horses. But Ahab — oh, he's a hard driver. Look, he's driven one leg to death and lamed the other for life, like a spavined horse, and now wears out bone legs by the cord. Hello, there, you Smut! Lend a hand there with those screws, and let's finish it before the resurrection fellow comes calling with his horn for all legs, true or false, the way brewery-men go round collecting old beer barrels to fill them up again. What a leg this is! It looks like a real live leg, filed down to nothing but the core; he'll be standing on this tomorrow; he'll be taking altitudes on it. Hello! I almost forgot the little oval slate, smoothed ivory, where he figures up the latitude. So, so; chisel, file, and sandpaper, now!

items.reason: 'Hereby the casks are sought to be kept damply tight' (the aim) was made a fact: 'the casks are kept damply tight'.
items.new: *In sperm-whalers with any considerable quantity of oil on board, it is a regular twice-weekly duty to run a hose into the hold and drench the casks with sea-water, which is afterward removed at varying intervals by the ship's pumps. In this way the aim is to keep the casks damp and tight; while from the changed character of the water pumped out, the sailors readily detect any serious leakage in the precious cargo.

items.new: "Captain Ahab is mistaken; it is I. The oil in the hold is leaking, sir. We must hoist the Burtons (the hoisting tackles) and break out the hold."

items.reason: 'Up Burtons and break out?' generalized to 'Rig up tackles'.
items.new: "Hoist the Burtons and break out? Now that we are nearing Japan — heave to here for a week to tinker a parcel of old hoops?"

items.reason: 'I'll not have the Burtons hoisted' generalized to 'tackles'.
items.new: "And I was not speaking or thinking of that at all. Begone! Let it leak! I'm all leaking myself. Aye! Leaks in leaks! Not only full of leaky casks, but those leaky casks are in a leaky ship; and that's a far worse plight than the Pequod's, man. Yet I don't stop to plug my leak; for who can find it in the deep-loaded hull; or how could anyone hope to plug it, even if found, in this life's howling gale? Starbuck! I'll not have the Burtons hoisted."

items.reason: Archaic inversion 'What cares Ahab?' left.
items.new: "Let the owners stand on Nantucket beach and outyell the typhoons. What does Ahab care? Owners, owners? You are always prattling to me, Starbuck, about those miserly owners, as if the owners were my conscience. But look here, the only real owner of anything is its commander; and listen, my conscience is in this ship's keel. On deck!"

items.new: "No, sir, not yet; I do beg you. And I do dare, sir — to be patient! Shall we not understand each other better than we have till now, Captain Ahab?"

items.new: "You are only too good a fellow, Starbuck," he said quietly to the mate; then, raising his voice to the crew: "Furl the topgallant-sails, and close-reef the topsails, fore and aft; back the main-yard; hoist the Burton, and break out in the main-hold."

items.reason: 'the Burtons were hoisted' generalized to 'tackles'; 'It were perhaps vain' left archaic; 'open disaffection' (disloyalty) changed to 'open defiance'.
items.new: It would perhaps be useless to guess exactly why Ahab acted this way toward Starbuck. It may have been a flash of honesty in him; or mere prudent policy which, under the circumstances, sternly forbade the slightest sign of open disaffection, however fleeting, in the important chief officer of his ship. However it was, his orders were carried out; and the Burtons were hoisted.
